Co-dev case study: How Blackbird Interactive and Secret Mode helped Escape the Backrooms ride the Backrooms hype wave
A co-dev partnership helped Fancy's hit game Escape The Backrooms reach over 4 million players.
Steven Messner
,
Director of Comms and Audiences
,
Blackbird Interactive
October 6, 2026
schedule
14 Min Read
Editor's note
: After our excellent conversation with Blackbird Interactive and other co-dev experts on the
Game Developer Podcast
, we wanted to know more about the process and planning of co-dev projects. Today's dev-authored piece explores how an experienced co-dev studio helped a solo-developed game reach new audiences and solve fundamental production challenges.
The Backrooms
is a creepypasta Cambrian Explosion of unprecedented scale. Over seven short years, it has ballooned into a shared universe encompassing massive wikis, viral videos, and a movie that just shattered several box office records (like best opening weekend for an original horror movie in history). All of this born from a single, eerie photograph posted on 4chan in 2019.
The Backrooms' influence on gaming has been no less pervasive. It almost single-handedly popularized the aesthetic of liminal spaces, becoming a clear reference point for other hit games like The Exit 8 (which also got its own film last year). On Steam,
there are over 270 released games
with at least one review that use Backrooms in their title—over 85 of them launching in 2025. But none of these projects have managed to eclipse the popularity of one game in particular:
Escape the Backrooms
.
Related:
Ubisoft Montreal employees launch collective action to preserve hybrid work schedule
With over 4 million players across PC, Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch 2,
Escape the Backrooms
has become the most popular way to explore this extradimensional, puke-yellow maze of fluorescent lights and musty carpet. It started as a side project of an amateur indie developer and YouTube creator. But, like the creepypasta that inspired it, Escape the Backrooms quickly snowballed into something much bigger.
It's dangerous to go alone...
The solo developer of
Escape the Backrooms
is an enigmatic person known only by his pseudonym, Fancy. He's an exceptionally rare breed of creator. The type who can somehow juggle school and a part-time job while also running a highly-successful
YouTube channel
and
solo develop a hit video game. No biggie.
Escape the Backrooms
hit Steam Early Access in August of 2022 and peaked just shy of 1,000 concurrent players (CCU). Months prior, Fancy had released a pair of YouTube devlogs that each earned millions of eyeballs apiece. That success compounded significantly over the next two years across three major updates, two seasonal events, and 22 hotfixes. When Fancy released the Part 4 update in January of 2024, Escape the Backrooms peaked at 16.5K CCU. But then that progress ground to a halt as he set out to port the games to consoles.
Related:
'We were constantly overshooting our capacity:' Arc Raiders exec says success resulted in burnout
In an August 2025
video
and
Steam blog
, Fancy revealed that he had hit a wall: Despite pouring all his free time and energy into it, developing content while also porting
Escape the Backrooms
to consoles (in addition to making videos and keeping the community up to date) was simply too many hats for one person to wear. So, he had taken time out of developing to find a partner who could take over the project and help him get it done.
Fancy announced he'd joined forces with
Secret Mode
, the UK-based publisher of games like
Chained Together
,
Still Wakes the Deep
, and the upcoming
Star Wars: Galactic Racer
. While Secret Mode was equipped to take over publishing and marketing for
Escape the Backrooms
, it still needed an external team to own development and help with the exponentially growing list of programming and engineering challenges behind bringing a multiplayer game to current gen consoles. Thankfully, Secret Mode didn't have to look far.
Amid the tectonic shifts that continue to rock the games industry, we at BBI found stability in leveraging the unique expertise of our veteran teams through co-development. Though we started as a 30-person, boutique studio, we now are home to 200 staff spread across a range of incredible partnerships like Starfield's recent Free Lanes and Terran Armada updates,
Subnautica's
Switch ports, numerous Minecraft partnerships and our own original games like
Hardspace: Shipbreaker
.
Related:
Microsoft CEO says Xbox is simply 'streamlining' after cutting over 5,750 jobs in three years
Typically, co-development engagements involve a lengthy process where a request for proposal (RFP) is circulated among networks of vendors. They compete across budget, expertise, and creative proposals to prove why they're the perfect partner to enlist. Our involvement with
Escape the Backrooms
unfolded slightly differently: BBI and Secret Mode had recently become sibling organizations through a mutual investment partner in Emona Capital.
Working together was already something we were both keen to do, and once we took the time to understand Secret Mode's ambitions and timelines for
Escape the Backrooms
, we felt strongly that we had the right people and processes to make it a reality. Soon after, Project Minotaur, our internal codename, was formally kicked off. Now we just had to execute, and our first major deadline was fast approaching.
Into The Backrooms
Work on Project Minotaur formally began in September 2025. The initial project scope was broken down into three core pieces:
● Ship 1.0 on PC, Xbox, and PS5 by October 23.
● Develop a Switch 2 version from scratch to launch early 2026.
● Add new features and improvements through regular content updates to bridge the gap
The team started with just two staff: One producer and a lead engineer doing foundational work necessary before
